paragraphs: From erythrocytosis to WHO-defined polycythemia vera

Erythrocytosis means an increased red-cell concentration, usually recognized by an elevated hemoglobin or hematocrit. It may reflect a true increase in red-cell mass (absolute erythrocytosis) or a reduction in plasma volume (relative erythrocytosis).

Clinical manifestations are often nonspecific and relate to impaired microvascular flow and blood hyperviscosity, with complications that include arterial and venous thrombosis, paradoxical bleeding, and progressive symptom burden.
Red-cell mass rises because EPO or hypoxia stimulates a normal clone
OSA(obstructive sleep apnea), hypoxia, smoking/carboxyhemoglobin, cardiopulmonary disease, high altitude, renal/hepatic tumors, exogenous EPO/androgens, and oxygen-sensing pathway disorders.
Dehydration, diuretics, stress erythrocytosis or Gaisböck erythrocytosis
Red-cell mass rises because a marrow clone produces cells independently of EPO (low EPO levels)
PV (usually JAK2-driven), Primary familial and congenital polycythemia
The reference ranges for normal hemoglobin and hematocrit vary by altitude, ethnicity, and country.

However, for reference, the hemoglobin and hematocrit values for a healthy adult man are 16 g/dL ± 2 g/dL and 47% ± 6%, respectively. The hemoglobin and hematocrit of a menstruating adult woman are usually 13 g/dL± 2 gm/dL and 40%± 6%, respectively.
Polycythemia in newborns is defined as a central venous hematocrit greater than 65% or a hemoglobin value greater than 22 g/dL.
The problem is concentration too little plasma around a near-normal red-cell mass
It is classically described in middle-aged men and is associated with obesity, cigarette smoking, hypertension, stress, and diuretic use.

The diagnosis is one of exclusion. Persistent erythrocytosis should first be distinguished from PV and secondary absolute erythrocytosis caused by hypoxia, erythropoietin-producing disorders, medications, or other underlying conditions.
Severe dehydration due to isolated fluid loss
increased hemoglobin and hematocrit may reflect diarrhea or severe vomiting.
True polycythemia is further stratified based on serum erythropoietin (EPO) levels.
Absolute PRIMARY polycythemia (Low serum EPO levels):
Low oxygen delivery or excess EPO → kidney / tissue signal → marrow erythropoiesis
Expected pattern: EPO normal or high; JAK2 absent; no clonal panmyelosis.
OSA, COPD, cyanotic heart disease, smoking/CO, altitude
Renal/hepatic lesions, rare tumors, exogenous EPO
Absolute SECONDARY erythrocytosis(High serum EPO levels):
Respiratory disorders: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, obesity hypoventilation syndrome (formerly Pickwickian syndrome), uncontrolled asthma
Renal disorders: Renal cysts, kidney cancer, renal artery stenosis
Elevated carboxyhemoglobin: Usually seen in individuals who smoke tobacco or those with occupational exposure (working on cars in enclosed spaces or in broiler rooms)
Hemoglobinopathies: High-affinity hemoglobins such as hemoglobin Yakima (a rare, inherited hemoglobin variant with high oxygen affinity)
EPO-secreting tumors: Hepatocellular carcinoma, uterine leiomyomas, and cerebellar hemangioblastomas
Iatrogenic causes: Erythropoietin analog administration, anabolic steroids, or testosterone replacement therapy
Absolute secondary erythrocytosis — EPO or drug-driven:
The laboratory goal is to prove an external driver and avoid mislabeling the patient as PV

Neonates typically have higher hematocrit levels than adults; this increase is a normal compensatory mechanism in newborns due to relative intrauterine tissue hypoxia. Neonatal polycythemia is exacerbated by the high affinity of fetal hemoglobin for oxygen.
Think germline when the phenotype is lifelong, familial or unexplained after acquired causes are excluded.
PART 4 — PV: absolute primary acquired erythrocytosis
Hb >16.5 g/dL or Hct >49% in men;
Hb >16.0 g/dL or Hct >48% in women.

The primary defect in nearly 95% of cases of polycythemia vera is an acquired mutation in exon 14 of the Janus kinase 2 (JAK2) gene (V617F). Mutations have also been described in exon 12 of the JAK2 gene. These mutations disrupt the inhibitory regulation of the pseudo kinase domain, leading to constitutive signaling. This constitutive activation results in both hypersensitivity to EPO and EPO-independent erythroid colony formation.

Cellular hypoxia can occur due to any causes that triggers the release of erythropoietin from the renal peritubular interstitial fibroblast-like cells. A small amount of EPO is also produced by the liver. Erythropoietin then acts on erythroid progenitor cells, stimulating erythropoiesis.
Because the clone affects more than red-cell production, PV may show leukocytosis, thrombocytosis, splenomegaly, pruritus and constitutional symptoms
The prevalence of polycythemia vera is approximately 22 cases per 100,000 population.
No consistent or clinically meaningful differences in incidence have been demonstrated across racial or ethnic groups.
Polycythemia vera shows a slight male predominance (male-to-female ratio approximately 1.2 to 1.5:1).
Polycythemia vera is most commonly diagnosed after age 50, but younger adults may be affected.
In contrast, polycythemia due to hemoglobinopathies and congenital cyanotic heart diseases is usually detected in younger patients.

This condition can be associated with over production of all 3 cell lines, with a notable predilection for red blood cells. The manifestations of erythrocytosis, regardless of cause, typically stem from the associated risks of blood hyperviscosity, including thrombotic events. Paradoxically, bleeding events are also frequently reported. Additionally, the rare risk of leukemic transformation, particularly after long-term cytotoxic therapy, may influence management.
Phlebotomy has been established as the backbone of therapy.
Hydroxyurea is usually considered second-line therapy.
The JAK2 inhibitor ruxolitinib is used when patients are intolerant or unresponsive to hydroxyurea.
